title: The Little Bear and the Storm
summary: One stormy night, the thunder frightens little Nilo. Mama Bear teaches him a trick for knowing when the storm is going away.

scenes.text:
In a little house in the forest lived Nilo and Mama Bear.

That night it was raining. The drops tapped on the roof, tick, tick, tick, and slid down the windowpanes as if they were having a race.

Nilo was already in bed, his eyes nearly closed.

And suddenly…

BOOM!

Nilo jumped. His ears shot up. He leapt out of bed and ran to hide in Mama's lap.

"What was that?"

"Thunder," said Mama Bear, hugging him tight. "There's a storm."

Nilo was trembling. His heart was going thump-thump, thump-thump, very fast.

"I don't like thunder," he said. "It's so big. And I never know when it's going to come."

Mama Bear sat down with him by the window and wrapped him in the blanket.

"Shall I teach you a trick? It's a trick for measuring the storm."

"You can measure it?"

"Look. First you see a light in the sky. Then comes the thunder. If you count slowly how long it takes, you'll know if the storm is near or far."

Just then, the whole window lit up with a flash of lightning.

"One…" counted Mama Bear. "Two…"

And far away, the thunder rumbled.

"Two," said Mama Bear. "It's close, but not right on top of us. And now comes the second part of the trick: while you count, you breathe. Breathe in on one number. Breathe out on the next."

Nilo breathed in. He breathed out. He breathed in. He breathed out.

His heart began to calm down. Thump… thump… thump.

And once again, out there, came a flicker.

"One," counted Nilo, all by himself this time. "Two. Three. Four…"

The thunder was quieter.

"Four!" said Nilo. "I counted to four!"

"And what does that mean?"

"That it's further away!"

The rain kept falling, but now Nilo watched the window without hiding. He was waiting for the next light.

There it was. Far away behind the trees, a tiny glimmer.

"One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six…"

This time the thunder was just a grumble, like a cat under the sofa.

"Six!" shouted Nilo, bouncing in Mama's lap. "It's going away! The storm is going away!"

"It's going away," said Mama Bear, and she kissed him between the ears. "And you walked it all the way to the door."

Little by little, the rain grew lighter. It wasn't drumming on the roof any more: it was stroking it.

Nilo kept watching the window, his eyes getting heavier and heavier.

"I'm going to count the next one," he said, yawning. "One… two…"

But he never got to three.

He fell asleep in Mama's lap, wrapped in the blanket, with a warm nose and a calm heart.

Mama Bear carried him to bed without waking him.

"Goodnight, my brave one," she whispered.

And outside, far away, the storm went on its way, without a sound.
